query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a graded Inconel 718 transition interlayer onto the high-entropy alloy (HEA) intermediate layer will enhance heat-transfer capability while maintaining the structural integrity of plasma‐facing components under reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An HEA intermediate layer that, while mechanically robust, currently exhibits suboptimal thermal conduction and experiences interfacial stresses due to mismatched thermal expansion with its adjoining materials.
generation.intervention: Introduce a graded Inconel 718 transition interlayer via laser cladding onto the HEA coating.
generation.conditions: Service conditions typical of plasma-facing components, with operating temperatures in the range of approximately 300°C to 700°C, high heat fluxes, and cyclic thermal loading.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded interlayer acts as a buffer that gradually bridges the thermal expansion differences between the HEA and the adjacent substrate, thereby reducing interfacial stresses and minimizing the risk of crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: Inconel 718 is known for its excellent thermal expansion matching, high thermal conductivity, and robust mechanical properties. By grading this layer onto the HEA, the interlayer facilitates improved heat conduction across the interface while its graded composition mitigates thermal mismatch stresses that can initiate damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to HEA intermediate layers without the graded interlayer, the modified structure should exhibit a lower thermal gradient (improved effective heat-transfer), reduced thermal stress-induced damage (fewer interfacial cracks or delaminations), and overall improved durability under reactor operating conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional HEA intermediate layers that lack a graded transition interlayer tend to develop significant thermal resistance and are more prone to interfacial degradation during rapid thermal cycling.
generation.boundary: The anticipated performance enhancement is contingent on achieving a uniform graded deposition; deviations in the interlayer thickness or composition may reduce the effectiveness. Additionally, if operational temperatures significantly exceed the stability range of Inconel 718, the benefits may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies indicate excellent thermal expansion matching and bonding for Inconel 718 in similar applications, the precise magnitude of heat-transfer improvement and stress reduction in the specific HEA system remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sample sets: one with the HEA intermediate layer paired with the graded Inconel 718 transition interlayer deposited via laser cladding, and a control set with the standard HEA intermediate layer only. Subject both sets to thermal cycling (ramping between 300°C and 700°C) and high heat-flux conditions simulating plasma-facing reactor environments.
measurements: Mapping of thermal conductivity across the interface using infrared thermography and/or laser flash analysis
Interfacial integrity assessment via three-point bending tests and microscopic evaluation for crack propagation
Post-exposure microstructural analysis using SEM/XRD to assess phase stability and bonding quality
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graded Inconel 718 interlayer does not produce a statistically significant increase in effective heat transfer (i.e., reduced thermal gradients) and fails to lower the incidence of interfacial damage relative to the control HEA sample under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis study addresses the crack formation problem when laser cladding CoCrFeNiAl high-entropy alloy onto H13 hot-work die steel, aiming to identify suitable transition layer materials. Five nickel-based alloys—Inconel 718, Inconel 625, Hastelloy X, FGH4096, and FGH4169—are selected as alternatives. Three-point bending and hot tensile tests are conducted to assess performance under different stress directions. Test results show that the FGH4096 and FGH4169 coatings fail due to insufficient element diffusion and weak interfacial bonding. Cracks appear at the coating–substrate interface of Inconel 625 and Hastelloy X. In contrast, Inconel 718 performs best, with excellent thermal expansion matching and strong stress resistance. In the three-point bending test, the specimens with Inconel 718 transition layers did not show cracks during the loading process, while specimens with some other alloy transition layers cracked or fractured, which proves that Inconel 718 can effectively enhance the bonding force between the coating and the substrate and improve the material’s performance under bending stress. Nickel-based alloys have emerged as the preferred materials for transition coatings between CoCrFeNiAl high-entropy alloys and H13 steel substrates, owing to their optimal thermal expansion coefficient matching, excellent chemical compatibility, favorable wettability, and superior mechanical properties []. Specifically, Inconel 718, Inconel 625, Hastelloy X, FGH4096, and FGH4169, as representative nickel-based superalloys, demonstrate well-matched thermal expansion coefficients with both the high-entropy alloy coating and H13 steel substrate. This compatibility significantly reduces thermal stress and minimizes the risk of cracking in the heat-affected zone during laser-cladding processes []. Regarding chemical compatibility, these alloys exhibit remarkable stability against interfacial reactions with both CoCrFeNiAl high-entropy alloys [] and H13 tool steels [] at elevated processing temperatures. Furthermore, each alloy possesses distinct strengthening mechanisms (e.g., solid solution strengthening, precipitation hardening) that ensure exceptional mechanical performance under service conditions.

chosen.approach: Designing HEA cladding coatings with optimized interlayers
